challenges.name: structured-output-quiz
challenges.title: Structured output: validate before you use it
challenges.description: Two recorded answers of the hint model: one that type-checks but is not what the type says, and one cut short with structured output turned on.

questions.explanation: False. JSON.parse returns any, and any can be assigned to HintAnswer without a single check, so the compiler has nothing to complain about. Types are erased at runtime: the object that reaches the page is exactly what the model wrote, with level as the string "2". On the page, level === 2 is false, a switch over level falls through to its default branch, and "2" + 1 is "21". The type annotation is a claim about the value, not a check of it; only code that looks at the value at runtime (a validator, a schema library) turns the claim into a fact. The misconception is that a clean tsc run covers data that arrives at runtime: from the network, from the database or from a model.

Statement: "Even with structured output turned on, this response must go through the server's validator, and the validator should reject it before the lesson page sees it."
questions.explanation: True. The log says the model stopped because it reached the output token limit (stopReason max_tokens), so the JSON was cut in the middle of a string and will not even parse. Structured output features make a valid answer much more likely, but a response can still be truncated, a fallback model may not support the feature, a refusal can come back in another shape, and which schema keywords a provider enforces differs between providers (check the provider's current docs). The validator is the only place that knows for sure, so the server checks every answer and turns a broken one into a typed error (retry or fallback is the next module) instead of a crash on the page. The misconception is that asking for a schema is the same as getting one.

challenges.name: validate-hint-json
challenges.title: Validate the hint model's JSON output
challenges.description: The hint model is asked to answer with JSON for { hint, level, references, revealsSolution }. The old service did `JSON.parse(text.match(/\{[\s\S]*\}/)![0]) as HintAnswer`; one answer came wrapped in prose with "level": "2", the cast let it through and the lesson page crashed. Write parseHintAnswer(text) that returns { ok: true, value } with a HintAnswer, or { ok: false, errors } with every problem found. Rules, in this order: (1) Trim text. If the whole trimmed text is one fence, take only its content: the first line is ``` or ```json (json in any case, spaces or tabs allowed after it), the last line is ```, and lines may end with \n or \r\n. Anything before or after the fence means the text is not a fence. Do not search for JSON inside prose. (2) If JSON.parse fails, the only error is "$: not valid JSON". (3) If the value is not a plain object (null, an array, a string, a number), the only error is "$: expected an object". (4) Otherwise collect errors: first "$.<key>: unexpected key" for each key that is not one of the four, in the order of the object's keys; then the four fields in this order. hint: "$.hint: required" when the key is absent, "$.hint: expected a string", "$.hint: must not be blank" (empty or only whitespace), "$.hint: longer than 400 characters" (string length; exactly 400 is allowed). level: "$.level: required" or "$.level: expected 1, 2 or 3" (only the numbers 1, 2 and 3; the string "2" is an error). references: "$.references: required", "$.references: expected an array", or, for an array, "$.references: more than 3 items" when it has more than 3, then "$.references[<i>]: expected a string" for every item that is not a string. revealsSolution: "$.revealsSolution: required" or "$.revealsSolution: expected a boolean". A key that is present with the value null is not absent: it gets the type error. Each field gets at most one error, except the items of references. (5) With no errors, value is a new object with exactly the four fields. revealsSolution: true is valid here: deciding what to do with it is the service's job, not the validator's. No libraries, and no `as HintAnswer`. The runner reads a list of raw outputs and prints the list of results as JSON.
hints: Which questions have to be answered before you can look at a single field: is there a fence around the whole text, is it JSON at all, is it an object? And once you reach the fields, should the first problem end the check, or should you keep going so the log shows everything that was wrong?

Look at four tools: a regular expression anchored at both ends (^ at the start and $ at the end, with a capture group for the content) for the fence; try/catch around JSON.parse with the result typed as unknown; a type guard isRecord(v) that rules out null and arrays; and Object.prototype.hasOwnProperty.call(obj, key) to tell an absent key from a key whose value is null. Object.keys(obj) gives the keys in their order for the unexpected-key check.

The same steps on a different schema, { severity: "info" | "warning"; line: integer >= 1 }, for the input {"severity":"error","line":"12","author":"bot"}: the keys are severity, line, author, so the first error is "$.author: unexpected key"; severity is present but not allowed -> "$.severity: expected info or warning"; line is a string -> "$.line: expected an integer >= 1". Three errors, returned together. For {"severity":"info"} the only error is "$.line: required". For [1, 2] the only error is "$: expected an object", and the fields are never looked at.
